A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the time complexity of broadcasting with omission failures is similar to that of the fault-free case (up to a log n factor), while for Byzantine failures the time complexity is significantly worse, and the gap is even larger when broadcasting is required with high probability.
for almost-safe broadcasting, the radio model is more robust than the message passing model, but it is also harder to design efficient algorithms for the radio model.
the complexity of almost-safe broadcast in both models is O (D + log α(n) n), where D is a parameter of the network and α(n) is an increasing function in n.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the feasibility of almost-safe broadcasting is independent of the failure model (i.e., omission vs. Byzantine), but its complexity depends on the failure model.

, while the message passing model is much more powerful than the radio model in terms of fault-tolerant communication, the latter is still capable of almost-safe broadcasting with a small overhead, for both types and both models of failures.
